section.title: The Voice of the Lord
section.sectionRationale: A hymn of David that pictures a great storm rolling in from the sea and sweeping across the land as the very voice of the LORD, calling heavenly beings to ascribe glory to Him, and closing with the LORD enthroned as King forever, who gives His people strength and peace.
section.thesis: The sevenfold voice of the LORD, thundering with power over the cedars and the wilderness alike, proclaims that the same God enthroned over the flood as King forever is the one who gives strength and peace to His own people.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a call for heavenly beings to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD (1-2); the sevenfold voice of the LORD thundering through the storm, climaxing in the cry of 'Glory' in His temple (3-9); and the LORD enthroned as King forever, giving strength and peace to His people (10-11).

units.label: Ascribe to the LORD glory and strength
units.note: a call to the heavenly beings

verses.text: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD {{kavod|glory}} and strength.
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness.

The {{qol|voice}} of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders; 
the LORD is heard over many waters.
The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is majestic.
The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon.
He makes Lebanon skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox.
The voice of the LORD strikes with flames of fire.
The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh.

The voice of the LORD twists the oaks and strips the forests bare. 
And in His temple all cry, "Glory!"

units.label: The LORD is enthroned as King forever
units.note: strength and peace for His people

verses.text: The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever.
The LORD gives His people strength; the LORD blesses His people with {{shalom|peace}}.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, honor, the visible weightiness of God's presence and character. Heavenly beings are called to ascribe, to acknowledge in words, the glory that already and fully belongs to God.

qol.gloss: Voice, sound. Repeated seven times in this psalm, the voice of the LORD is inseparable from the LORD Himself, His speech accomplishing exactly what it declares, a pattern that culminates in the eternal Word who was with God and was God, John 1:1.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being, more than the absence of conflict. The same voice that shatters cedars and shakes the wilderness is the voice that blesses God's people with this full, settled peace.

basic.context: David calls the heavenly beings to ascribe to the LORD the glory and strength due His name. A great storm then rises over the Mediterranean Sea and sweeps east over the land, and the psalm pictures this storm as the voice of the LORD, thundering, breaking cedars, shaking the wilderness, until in God's temple all creation cries out, 'Glory!' The psalm closes with the LORD enthroned over the flood as King forever, who gives His people strength and blesses them with peace.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read as worship shaped by the natural world's testimony to God's power, not nature worship itself; the storm does not compete with the LORD but is simply His voice, and the psalm's real center is not meteorology but praise.
basic.originalLanguages: The heavenly beings are called to ascribe kavod, glory, weighty honor, to the LORD. His qol, voice, is repeated seven times, inseparable from His own person and power, and the psalm closes with the LORD giving His people shalom, full and settled peace, not merely calm weather but wholeness of life.
basic.typology: The voice of the LORD that thunders with creative and destructive power anticipates the eternal Word, John 1:1, through whom all things were made, and the same voice that stills or stirs the sea anticipates Jesus, who speaks and even wind and sea obey Him, Mark 4:39-41.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Word, the voice of the LORD made flesh, John 1:1, 14, through whom all things were created and by whose word the disciples watched wind and sea obey instantly, Mark 4:39-41, provoking the same question this psalm answers, 'Who then is this?' He is also the King enthroned forever, fulfilling verse 10's vision of the LORD reigning over the flood, and the giver of the true peace this psalm closes with, not as the world gives, John 14:27.
basic.god: God's voice is shown as inseparable from His own power and presence, capable of both overwhelming, world-shaking force and tender blessing, giving strength and peace to the very people who might otherwise tremble at His majesty.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:1-3 identifies Jesus as the eternal Word through whom all things were made, echoing this psalm's voice that shapes creation. Mark 4:39-41 shows Jesus commanding wind and sea with a word, provoking wonder at who He must be. John 14:27 shows Jesus giving His own peace, not as the world gives, fulfilling the psalm's closing blessing.
basic.oneStory: The sevenfold voice of the LORD that thunders through the storm and shakes creation, while all in His temple cry 'Glory,' finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the eternal Word through whom all things were made, who commands wind and sea, reigns as King forever, and gives His people true and lasting peace.

context.literary:
Psalm 29 is built on repetition, and the repetition does the arguing. The imperative 'ascribe' opens the psalm three times, verses 1 and 2, and the phrase 'the voice of the LORD' opens seven lines between verses 3 and 9. The name of the LORD, Yahweh, sounds again and again through the psalm, so the poem is soaked in the divine name from the first word to the last. The last verse returns to the vocabulary of the first, 'strength', so the psalm forms a ring: strength is ascribed to the LORD at the start, and the LORD gives strength to His people at the end.

The structure has three panels. The first, verses 1 and 2, is a summons on earth's edge to heaven's court. The second, verses 3 to 9, is a report of a storm, in the present tense, as if the psalmist were standing under it. The third, verses 10 and 11, is the verdict, that the LORD is enthroned as King and gives peace. The storm section is packed with movement: it begins over the waters, in verse 3, then advances to the cedars of Lebanon and Sirion in the north, verses 5 and 6, and sweeps down to the wilderness of Kadesh in the south, verse 8. Many readers note that the storm is traced across the whole land, north to south, so that the entire country is claimed.

Within the seven lines of the storm the sounds change. The first is over the waters, the second is powerful and majestic, and the middle ones break, shake and strip. Verse 9 is the turning point. The second half of that verse, 'And in His temple all cry, "Glory!"', is the only line in the storm section that does not begin with 'the voice of the LORD', and it interrupts the thunder with the answer of the worshippers. The psalm's first word to the heavenly beings, 'ascribe glory', is now fulfilled, so the poem closes its own circle at the exact moment the storm reaches its peak.

The final two verses carry the conclusion in two short sentences that are balanced against each other: He sits as King, and He gives strength and peace. The great power of the storm and the gift of peace belong to one Person.
context.historical:
The psalm belongs to the world of the ancient Near East, where storms mattered. Farmers in Canaan depended on the rains that came from the Mediterranean in winter, and Israel's neighbours worshipped a storm god, Baal, who was said to ride the clouds and to speak in thunder. Ancient texts from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast, show that this language was current. An Israelite hearing Psalm 29 would have known that these were the words other peoples used of Baal, and the psalm makes the claim that the voice in the thunder belongs to the LORD.

The geography traces the whole width of Israel's world. The waters of verse 3 are the open sea. Lebanon and Sirion, verses 5 and 6, are the northern mountains, and Sirion is the name the Sidonians used for Hermon, Deuteronomy 3:9. The cedars of Lebanon were the tallest and most valuable trees known to Israel and were used for kings' houses and for the temple, so to see them broken was to see the mightiest thing on earth broken. The wilderness of Kadesh in verse 8 is usually placed in the south, in the region where Israel wandered after Egypt, Numbers 20:1. A storm that passes through both ends of the land leaves no place untouched.

Israel also knew the voice of the LORD in thunder from its own history. At Sinai there was thunder and lightning and a loud trumpet, Exodus 19:16, and the people trembled. When the Philistines came against Israel at Samuel's sacrifice, the LORD 'thundered loudly against the Philistines', 1 Samuel 7:10, and Hannah sang that He would 'thunder from heaven' against those who oppose Him, 1 Samuel 2:10. Storm was one of the ways that God had shown Himself in Israel's memory.

The final scene is set in the temple, and the psalm likely belonged to public worship. In later Jewish practice it was sung on the eve of the Sabbath, and the last verse was used as a blessing of the people when the scroll of the law was carried back to its place. The psalm has always been heard as the song of a community more than of a private believer.
context.canonical:
Psalm 29 is one of the great enthronement psalms, and it is set in a family of texts that picture the LORD reigning over the waters. Psalm 93 begins 'The LORD reigns!', speaks of floodwaters that have raised their voice, and says that the LORD on high is majestic above the roar of many waters, Psalm 93:1 to 4. Psalm 46:3 has the waters roar and foam while God is a refuge. The pictures are consistent: the sea, which the ancient world feared, is beneath the throne.

The opening call was so loved that it was borrowed. 1 Chronicles 16:28 to 29 and Psalm 96:7 to 9 repeat the words 'Ascribe to the LORD glory and strength' and 'Worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness', with a change: in those two places the summons is addressed to 'the families of the nations' rather than the heavenly beings. The psalm was therefore heard as a call that would grow from heaven to earth.

Thunder as the voice of God fills the Old Testament. Job hears the LORD 'thunder wondrously with His voice', Job 37:2 to 5; David sings that the LORD thundered from heaven and the voice of the Most High resounded, Psalm 18:13; and the psalm of Asaph recalls the thunder in the whirlwind, Psalm 77:18. In Elijah's experience at Horeb, the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice, 1 Kings 19:11 to 12, and the contrast shows that God's voice is not confined to one form.

In the New Testament the Father's voice comes from heaven at the baptism of Jesus, over the waters, Matthew 3:16 to 17, and again in the temple courts when some in the crowd said it had thundered, John 12:28 to 29. John hears 'the seven thunders' speak in Revelation 10:3 to 4, and the throne room has 'flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder', Revelation 4:5, and a multitude shouts 'Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns,' Revelation 19:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted Israel to look at a storm and see a King. In the ancient world a thunderstorm was terrifying and mysterious, and many peoples answered it with worship of a storm god. The psalm takes the thing that frightened everyone and gives it a name: this is the voice of the LORD. The first hearers were to walk out under the sky and not be afraid of the forces of nature or of any rival god, because all of it answers to one Voice.

He also wanted them to see that this power is not a threat to His people. The storm smashes cedars, but the last verse says that the same LORD gives His people strength and blesses them with peace. The thing that would be terror to His enemies is a source of strength to them. The psalm places the sanctuary in the storm's very midst, 'And in His temple all cry, "Glory!"', to say that the safe place is not away from the thunder but under the King who sends it.

The call to the heavenly beings at the start has a purpose too. If even the mightiest beings in heaven are to give glory to the LORD, then the tribes of Israel can worship without fear that a higher power is watching. The psalm is an instruction in whom to fear and in whom to trust, and it ends with peace, for the first hearers were meant to leave the sanctuary not shaken but steadied.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a storm and the response of praise to it. It records that God's voice is heard in thunder and that the heavens cry glory; it does not command a believer to see God's voice in every weather event, and it gives no ground for claiming that a particular storm is a direct message about a particular sin. The Old Testament itself is careful here: Job's friends assumed a storm meant judgment and were rebuked, Job 42:7.

What the psalm prescribes is worship. The imperative 'ascribe' is repeated three times, and that is the instruction that carries over: give the LORD the glory due His name, and worship in the splendor of His holiness. The rest of the psalm supplies the reasons.

It also has a quiet lesson about how believers use nature. The psalm does not tell us to worship the storm, and it does not say that nature is divine; it says that the storm is only His voice, and that the LORD is enthroned above the flood. Paul says the same when he writes that God's eternal power has been clearly seen in what has been made, Romans 1:20, and warns against worshipping the creation in place of the Creator. To stand in awe at the thunder and to offer thanks to the God who made it is a right response, and the psalm invites it.

debates.question: Was Psalm 29 adapted from a Canaanite hymn to the storm god Baal?

views.label: Yes, in part: an older storm-god hymn was reworked in praise of the LORD
views.case: Since the discovery of texts at Ugarit, some scholars have argued that the psalm's images, Lebanon, the thunder, the enthronement over the flood and the heavenly assembly, resemble the language used of Baal. Israel would then have taken familiar poetry and made it a claim: the LORD, not Baal, is the God of the storm.

views.label: No: it is an Israelite psalm that uses common images of storm and sea
views.case: Storm language was widespread in the ancient world, and a thunderstorm needs a certain vocabulary wherever it is described. The psalm is thoroughly grounded in the LORD's name and in Israel's own worship, and its use of thunder matches Israel's own tradition at Sinai and elsewhere, Exodus 19:16, 1 Samuel 7:10.

views.label: It is a polemic: the shared imagery is used to deny the rival's claims
views.case: Whether or not the psalm has an earlier source, it stands in a pointed relation to the Baal traditions. By giving to the LORD alone the voice, the cedars, the flood and the throne, it says that none of these belongs to another god.

debates.bearing: On every view the theological point is the same. The voice in the storm is the LORD's, and no rival can be given credit for it. A reader who worries about pagan parallels can note that Scripture uses common language to make uncommon claims.

debates.question: Who are the 'heavenly beings' addressed in verse 1?

views.label: The angels or members of God's heavenly court
views.case: The Hebrew phrase is 'sons of gods', and Psalm 89:6 asks 'Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD?' Job 38:7 speaks of the 'sons of God' shouting for joy. The scene of verse 1 is the court of heaven bowing to its King, as in Psalm 82:1, and the temple in verse 9 is the earthly echo of the heavenly one.

views.label: The rival gods of the nations, summoned to give up their claims
views.case: Some read the phrase as a summons to the gods that other peoples worship, told to ascribe glory to the LORD. This fits the polemic against Baal and Psalm 82:1, 'He renders judgment among the gods', and the New Testament sense that the powers will bow to Christ, Philippians 2:10 to 11.

views.label: The great ones of the earth, the powerful
views.case: The footnote notes another reading, 'sons of might', in which the call is to the mighty ones on earth, kings and rulers, and it matches the way the call was widened to nations in Psalm 96:7.

debates.bearing: The first reading has been the most common. Whichever is preferred, everything powerful in heaven or on earth is told to give the LORD the glory due His name.

debates.question: What is the 'flood' on which the LORD sits enthroned in verse 10?

views.label: The waters of Noah's flood
views.case: The Hebrew word mabbul is used elsewhere only in the account of Noah's flood, for example Genesis 6:17. On this reading the LORD who sat as judge over the deluge is the same LORD who sits over all catastrophe and reigns for ever.

views.label: The cosmic waters of chaos, tamed by God
views.case: In Psalm 93:3 to 4 and Psalm 46:3 the waters stand for the chaotic forces that threaten the world, and the LORD reigns above them. The flood is then the ancient world's symbol of everything that threatens order, and it is under His throne.

views.label: The storm itself
views.case: Others take the flood as the rain and the surging waters of the storm just described, so that verse 10 sums up the psalm: the LORD is King over the storm He has sent.

debates.bearing: All three converge on one point, that no flood, of water or of any other kind, is outside His rule, and the King who sits above it is not moved.

study.originalLanguages:
The phrase 'heavenly beings' in verse 1 is the Hebrew bene elim, literally 'sons of gods'. The BSB footnote gives 'sons of God' or 'sons of might' as alternatives, and Psalm 89:6 has the same expression. The plural form of the word for God, elim, keeps the phrase from being read as a single divine son and points to the members of the divine court. It is a powerful surprise to hear such beings being commanded, and the verb they are given is 'ascribe', from the Hebrew yahab, which is the ordinary verb for 'give'. They are told to give to the LORD what already belongs to Him, as a servant hands his master what is his. The command is repeated three times, and the repetition has the sound of a herald calling at a gate.

The phrase 'splendor of His holiness' in verse 2 is hadrat qodesh. The BSB footnote suggests 'in holy attire', because the noun hadarah can mean the beauty of clothing. Psalm 96:9 and 1 Chronicles 16:29 use the same phrase. Worship is dressed in the beauty of the holy.

When the psalm says 'the God of glory thunders' in verse 3, the verb is hir'im, from ra'am, 'to thunder', the same verb used of the LORD thundering against the Philistines in 1 Samuel 7:10. The verb makes the thunder something that God does. The word for voice, qol, means both a sound and a speech, and thunder is heard as speech.

In verse 6 the BSB says that Lebanon 'skips like a calf', and the verb is raqad, to skip or to dance. The mountains dance. The idea is not of a gentle skipping but of an earthquake-like shaking of the land, and the picture of a calf and a young wild ox shows the untamed leaping of young animals, so the mountains are made to behave like a herd.

Verse 9 contains a small puzzle noted by the BSB: the words translated 'twists the oaks' could also be read 'makes the deer to calve'. The Hebrew consonants allow either, depending on how one reads the vowels, and the first fits the parallel line, 'strips the forests bare', while the second suits the theme of the trembling of the wild. Either way the voice of the LORD reaches into the deepest part of the forest.

In the same verse the words rendered 'all cry, Glory' are kullo omer kavod, more literally 'everything in it says, Glory'. It may mean everyone in the temple, or everything in it, and it suggests a chorus in which no one stays silent.

The 'flood' of verse 10 is mabbul, a word that outside this verse belongs to the story of Noah's deluge, Genesis 6:17. The same verb, yashab, 'to sit', occurs in both halves of the verse, so the psalm says that He sits at the flood and sits as King for ever.

typology.type: The voice of the LORD over the waters, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: At creation God's word moved over the waters and light came into being, Genesis 1:3. In the gospel the voice of the Father sounds over the waters again at the baptism of Jesus, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:17, and the Spirit descends. The Word through whom all things were made, John 1:1 to 3, is the Son who is baptised. The type falls short of the reality because the psalm's voice only announces power, while at the Jordan the voice announces love for a Person.

typology.type: The voice that shakes the wilderness, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The shaking of the land by God's voice in the psalm is taken up in Hebrews 12:26, which recalls that at Sinai 'His voice shook the earth' and adds that He has promised to shake heaven as well. What follows in Hebrews is the promise of a kingdom that cannot be shaken, Hebrews 12:28. The type is completed in the reign of Christ, and it falls short because a storm passes, while the kingdom does not.

typology.type: The King enthroned over the flood, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: The LORD sits over the waters of judgment and chaos, and Jesus shows that authority in the boat: 'Silence! Be still!' Mark 4:39, so that the disciples ask who this is that the sea obeys, Mark 4:41. The one who rules the flood also rules over every power, for God raised Him and seated Him far above all rule and authority, Ephesians 1:21 to 22. The type falls short because the psalm sees the throne from below, whereas the gospel sees the Man who has sat down on it.

typology.type: The gift of strength and peace, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The blessing at the end of the psalm is the priestly blessing in a new form: 'the LORD... give you peace,' Numbers 6:26. Jesus gives what the psalm promises when He says, 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you,' John 14:27, and Paul says that being justified through faith we have peace with God, Romans 5:1. The type falls short in that the peace of the psalm was the calm of a people under a protecting King, whereas the peace of the gospel is a settled peace with God, secured by a cross.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through the voice. The seven statements of 'the voice of the LORD' present the voice as the way God acts in the world, and the opening of John's Gospel says that the Word who was with God and was God is the one through whom all things were made, John 1:1 to 3. Paul says that all things were created through Him and for Him, Colossians 1:16. The voice that shakes the wilderness and breaks the cedars is the voice of the pre-existent Word, and when that Word became flesh, John 1:14, His voice was heard in Galilee.

This is why the stilling of the storm carries such weight. When Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea, saying, 'Silence! Be still!' the wind died down and the sea was calm, Mark 4:39. The disciples were overwhelmed with fear and asked, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41. The answer that Psalm 29 gives is the LORD, whose voice is over the waters and who sits enthroned over the flood. Matthew's account has the same question: 'What kind of man is this?' Matthew 8:27. They are asking about a man and the psalm supplies the answer.

It leads to Christ by the baptism. The heavens were opened over the Jordan, and a voice came from heaven, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:16 to 17. The place is a river, the moment is one of glory, and the voice is the voice of the LORD. Near the end of His ministry, the Father's voice sounds again in the temple courts, and the crowd says it had thundered, John 12:28 to 29, which is exactly what Psalm 29 would lead a reader to expect.

It leads to Christ by the throne and the peace. The LORD is enthroned as King for ever, and the letter to the Ephesians says God seated Christ at His right hand far above all rule and authority, Ephesians 1:20 to 22. The last verse gives the people of the LORD strength and peace, and Jesus gives His own peace, 'not as the world gives', John 14:27, and says that in Him we may have peace even where there is tribulation, John 16:33. In the final book, the multitude sounds 'like a mighty rumbling of thunder' and cries that the Lord God the Almighty reigns, Revelation 19:6, so the thunder of the psalm becomes the thunder of the praise of the redeemed.

A caution guards the reading. Psalm 29 is about the LORD, and the reader should not make every tree and mountain a hidden portrait of Jesus. The New Testament draws the link at the Word, the voice, the stilling of the sea, and the enthroned King, and those links carry the weight.
study.god:
Psalm 29 shows a God whose glory is first His weight and then His voice. The psalm says almost nothing about His shape or place, but it speaks of what He does by speaking. The phrase 'the God of glory thunders' in verse 3 joins the two: glory is what He is, thunder is what He does. God's word is not information only, it is an act with force. He speaks and the cedars break.

It shows a God who is over nature without being part of it. The voice comes over the waters and passes through forests and mountains, but it is not the sea or the forest. The psalm belongs to the biblical insistence that the LORD is the Creator of the storm and not the storm itself, and that the forces the world fears are servants of His voice. Isaiah says heaven is His throne and earth His footstool, Isaiah 66:1, and the psalm sets that claim in motion.

It shows a God who commands the worship of all other powers. The heavenly beings are told to ascribe glory to Him, and the invitation is not a request. He does not share His glory with any other, and every claim of rival authority, in heaven or on earth, is under His name. That is a doctrine of His uniqueness, and it is the reason the Bible can say that none among the heavenly beings is like Him, Psalm 89:6.

It shows a God who reigns for ever. The King enthroned over the flood is not one who came to power after the flood, and He does not step down. Paul calls Him 'the King eternal, immortal, and invisible', 1 Timothy 1:17. His rule is not weakened by any chaos, and it is a rule that the psalm calls settled: 'enthroned as King forever'.

It shows a God who gives strength and peace to His people. The last verse is a surprise. After seven claps of thunder, the psalm ends in a blessing, which shows that the power of God and the kindness of God are one thing. His strength is not only for breaking cedars but for building up His people. The same God is awesome in His sanctuary and gives power and strength to His people, Psalm 68:35.

For worship, the psalm asks for awe that does not run away. We are to give Him the glory due His name and to worship in the beauty of holiness, and the last verse says we can do it without fear. The temple is the place where, even in the storm, everything says 'Glory'.

crossReferences.note: David's psalm of thanksgiving for the ark quotes the opening of Psalm 29 almost word for word but addresses the call to the families of the nations. It shows that the ascription of glory was understood as a duty that spreads from heaven to every people.

The same call, 'Ascribe to the LORD glory and strength', is offered to the nations and joined to an invitation to enter His courts and tremble before Him. It reads as an expansion of Psalm 29:1 to 2 for a wider audience.

'Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD?' The phrase for heavenly beings is the one in Psalm 29:1, and this verse states the point of the summons: none of them can be compared with the LORD, so they must give Him glory.

The LORD reigns, robed in majesty, and the floodwaters lift their voice, but He is more majestic than the roar of many waters. It is the closest neighbour to Psalm 29:10 in theme and shows that the enthronement over the flood was a settled part of Israel's worship.

The LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into confusion. The same verb for thundering is at work in Psalm 29:3, and the verse shows that the storm voice of the psalm was known in Israel as a weapon on behalf of God's people.

'The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded.' David describes God's rescue of him in storm language, making the point that the voice in the thunder is a voice that acts for the one who calls on Him.

Elihu tells Job to listen to the thunder of His voice, and says that God thunders wondrously and does great things we cannot comprehend. It is a wisdom parallel to Psalm 29, where the thunder teaches humility and awe.

At Sinai there was thunder and lightning and a loud trumpet, and the people trembled. The psalm's voice is the same voice that spoke the law, so the storm of Psalm 29 carries a memory of covenant, not only of nature.

The LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. It is a counterpoint to Psalm 29: the voice of God can thunder or whisper, and Psalm 29 does not deny the second while celebrating the first.

Jesus rebukes the wind and sea and they obey, and the disciples ask who He is. The sea that is under the LORD's throne in Psalm 29:10 is under the word of Jesus, and the question they ask is one that Psalm 29 has already answered.

A voice from heaven over the waters declares Jesus to be the beloved Son. The voice of the LORD over the waters in Psalm 29:3 is heard again at the baptism, and here it speaks not of thunder but of a Father's delight.

When the seven thunders sounded their voices, John was told to seal up what they said. The sevenfold voice of Psalm 29 has a counterpart in the last book, where the thunder of God is still heard, though its words are kept secret.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 29 gathers up the first act of the story and sets it before the whole creation. At the beginning God spoke, and light came, and the waters were divided, Genesis 1:3 to 10. The psalm's 'voice of the LORD over the waters' returns to that beginning and says that the same voice is heard now in every storm. The world is not a self-running machine, and the one who spoke at the start has not fallen silent.

The story goes on to the flood, where the waters of judgment rose over the earth, Genesis 7:11. The psalm's word for flood is the word that belongs to Noah's story, and to say that the LORD 'sits enthroned over the flood' is to say that the same King who judged the world and preserved a remnant rules over every catastrophe. That is why the psalm can end with peace. The God who is stronger than the flood is the one who gives strength to His people.

The middle of the story is Israel's, and it is a story in which the voice of the LORD is heard at Sinai and in the sanctuary, Exodus 19:16, and in which Israel learns to sing about a God greater than the gods of the nations. The psalm anticipates the worship of the nations: the words are borrowed for the call to the families of the earth, Psalm 96:7 to 9, and the promise to Abraham that all nations will be blessed is heard behind it.

The story turns in the Word who became flesh. The voice that made the world is the voice that stilled the storm, and the Son whom the Father names at the Jordan, over the waters, is the King enthroned. The peace of verse 11 is given in His name, John 14:27, and the church lives in that peace while the world still shakes.

The end of the story is a great sound. The multitude in Revelation roars like many waters and like thunder, 'Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns,' Revelation 19:6, and every creature in heaven and on earth ascribes to the Lamb 'power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing', Revelation 5:12. The temple in which everything cries 'Glory' is filled, and the people whom He blessed with peace stand in it. The thunder of Psalm 29 is never silenced, but it no longer terrifies.

quiz.q: Who is called to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD in verse 1?

options.note: The psalm opens by summoning the heavenly beings, not merely humans, to worship.

options.text: Only the kings of the earth.
options.note: The call is specifically to heavenly beings, not earthly kings, in this opening verse.

options.text: All the people of Israel gathered at worship.
options.note: Close, since Israel does ascribe glory to God elsewhere, but verse 1 specifically addresses heavenly beings, angelic beings, not the gathered human congregation.

options.text: No one; it is a private meditation.
options.note: The psalm opens with a direct, public call to worship, not private meditation.

quiz.q: How many times is the phrase 'the voice of the LORD' repeated in verses 3-9?

options.note: The sevenfold repetition structures the psalm's central section and its picture of the storm.
The repetition occurs seven times across these verses, more than three.
Close, an undercount by two, but the deliberate refrain 'the voice of the LORD' actually appears seven times across verses 3-9.
The correct count within this section is seven, not twelve.

quiz.q: What happens 'in His temple' according to verse 9?

options.note: This is the climactic response to the LORD's voice, worship breaking out in His temple.

options.text: All bow down in reverent silence, without any spoken response.
options.note: Close, since reverence is present, but the verse specifically describes a spoken, exultant cry, 'Glory,' not silent reverence.
The text specifies a cry of worship, 'Glory,' not a description of sacrificial ritual.
The verse describes a loud cry of worship, the opposite of silence.

quiz.q: What is the LORD said to be enthroned over in verse 10?

options.note: The verse pictures the LORD enthroned over the flood, and as King forever.

options.text: The nations of the earth only.
options.note: While the LORD reigns over the nations elsewhere in Scripture, this verse specifically names the flood.

options.text: The waters of the sea generally, without reference to a specific flood.
options.note: Close, since water imagery runs through the psalm, but verse 10 uses a specific term, the flood, echoing the great flood of Genesis, not water in general.
The verse explicitly says the LORD is enthroned, actively reigning, not hidden.

quiz.q: What two things does the LORD give His people in verse 11?

options.note: The psalm closes with this twofold blessing, strength and peace, for God's people.

options.text: Comfort and rest, without specific mention of strength.
options.note: Close in feeling, since comfort and rest are related to peace, but verse 11 specifically names strength alongside peace as the twofold gift.
This is the opposite of the blessing described, which is strength and peace.
The closing verse names strength and peace specifically, not material possessions.

questions: The psalm calls even heavenly beings to ascribe glory to the LORD. What in creation, a storm, the ocean, the night sky, most often moves you to worship rather than mere observation?

The voice of the LORD is powerful enough to shatter cedars and shake the wilderness, yet it is the same voice that blesses His people with peace. How do you hold together God's overwhelming power and His tender care in your own picture of Him?
In the temple, all creation's upheaval resolves into a single cry, 'Glory.' What in your life currently feels like upheaval, and how might worship reframe it rather than only fear or complaint?
The psalm insists the LORD alone, not any rival power, commands the storm. What competing sources of security or control are you tempted to trust instead of God's sovereign voice?
The psalm closes with strength and peace as gifts from God to His people. Where do you most need God's strength or peace this week, and how will you ask Him for it specifically?

translationNotes.note: Heavenly beings translates a Hebrew phrase literally meaning sons of God or sons of might, understood as angelic beings called to worship.
Sirion is another name for Mount Hermon, paired with Lebanon to describe the storm's path skipping across the region's great mountains like young animals.

Some manuscripts and translations render this line 'makes the oaks to shake' rather than describing deer giving birth, a matter of vowel pointing in the Hebrew consonantal text; either reading conveys the same overwhelming power of God's voice.
